pedagogy.summary: The right angle is the benchmark angle of Y3: a quarter turn, the corner of a square, marked with a small square. Children learn to identify it with a right-angle checker (folded paper / L-shape) and to classify other angles relative to it — less open or more open. The turn facet is quantitative: two right angles make a half turn, four make a complete turn (360°). The pedagogical goal is that the right angle becomes a reusable UNIT of comparison whose identity is independent of orientation and of arm length.
bestPractices: Make the checker: fold paper (or a circle) twice to build a right-angle tester and have children place it into real corners to test — a concrete, self-checking tool (NCETM 'Monster Right Angle Measurer').
Build right angles from turns: a quarter turn is one right angle, two quarter turns make a half turn (a straight line), four bring you back to the start; link to the four compass points.
Classify by comparison before naming: is this corner more open or less open than my checker? — establishing the less-than / greater-than idea informally ahead of the words acute/obtuse.
Vary orientation on purpose — rotate and mirror right angles off the upright — so 'right angle' is not tied to a standard L.
Connect the two facets: a quarter turn LEAVES a right angle between the start arm and the finish arm.
keyRepresentations: The right-angle checker / folded-paper tester, and the small-square right-angle mark
The clock face and compass rose showing quarter, half, three-quarter and full turns
Body turns and a hinge / geo-strip opened exactly to a right angle
The four right-angled corners of squares and rectangles
commonMisconceptions: A right angle must be 'upright' like a standard L; a rotated or mirrored one is not recognised as a right angle (orientation dependence)
A right angle drawn with long arms is 'bigger' or 'more than' one with short arms (the arm-length misconception carried over)
Any sharp-looking corner is a right angle — labelling corners by rough appearance rather than testing against the checker
Miscounting right angles in a turn — e.g. two right angles make a full turn, or a half turn returns you to the start

learn.summary: Year 3 children learn the right angle as a reusable benchmark unit: a quarter turn, the corner of a square, marked with a small square. They build and use a right-angle checker (folded paper / L-shape) to test real corners, classify other angles as less open or more open than a right angle, and compose turns from right angles (two make a half turn, four a complete turn / 360°). Key goal: the right angle's identity is independent of orientation and arm length.

activities.title: Make and use a right-angle checker
feedback: If the checker sits flush, it is a right angle — stamp the small square; a rectangular window corner should fit exactly.
If the corner is more open than a right angle, the checker's arm cannot reach the corner's other side and leaves a gap between them.

If the corner is less open than a right angle, the checker's arm overhangs past the corner's side — a pizza slice tip is usually less open than a right angle when the pizza is cut into more than four equal slices, but test it to check.
For the tilted right angle, turn the checker to match its orientation: it still fits exactly, so it is still a right angle — being 'on its side' does not change it.
For the long-armed corner, place the checker on both the long-armed and a short-armed right angle: both fit, so arm length does not make a corner 'bigger'.
(Adult note: the more-open case is an obtuse angle and the less-open case an acute angle; keep the child's language to 'more open' / 'less open' at this stage.)
activities.rationale: A concrete, self-checking tester lets children test rather than eyeball corners, intended to counter the 'sharp-looking = right angle' habit. Seeding tilted and long-armed right angles aims at the orientation-dependence and arm-length misconceptions; framing angle as opening (fit of the checker) rather than side length addresses the whole-object/side-length misconception, which the cited source notes is countered by framing angle as turn/opening.
sourceClaims: Recommended teaching reinforces that an angle is an amount of turn shown by two adjoining lines (one for the start, one for the finish); children make and use a right-angle tester (a 'Monster Right Angle Measurer') to find right angles in shapes and objects, and make right-angled turns between the four compass points.

Children judge angle size by irrelevant properties including the length of the sides (a same-size angle drawn with longer sides is judged bigger), a misconception robust from preschool through elementary years; it stems from a whole-object assumption and is countered by framing angle as the measure of turn/opening.
learnerActions: Fold a piece of paper (or a paper circle) in half and in half again to make a right-angle tester with a crisp square corner.
Place the checker into real corners around the room and on shapes — a window frame, a book corner, a slice of pizza, an open pair of scissors.
For each corner, decide: does the checker fit flush (a right angle), or is the corner less open / more open than the checker?
Mark each confirmed right angle with a small square symbol.
Deliberately test corners that are tilted off-upright and corners drawn with very long arms, turning the checker to match each corner before reading the fit.
activities.intendedInsight: A right angle is one reusable unit of comparison; a corner is a right angle only if it fits the checker exactly, regardless of how it is turned or how long its arms are.

activities.title: Build turns from right angles
feedback: If you predicted two turns to get home, notice that after two quarter turns in the same direction from your stated starting direction you are facing backwards — it takes four quarter turns in the same direction to return home.
After each quarter turn, confirm one right angle has been added; two make a half turn / straight line, four make 360°.
If you lose count, mark each quarter position on the floor or compass rose so the right angles stack visibly.
activities.rationale: Physically composing turns, with a prediction stated first against a named starting direction, surfaces the common miscount (that two right angles make a full turn, or that a half turn returns you to the start). Connecting the quarter turn to the static square corner joins the two facets of the concept.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should identify right angles, recognise that 2 right angles make a half-turn, 3 make three-quarters of a turn and 4 a complete turn, and identify whether angles are greater than or less than a right angle.

Recommended teaching reinforces that an angle is an amount of turn shown by two adjoining lines (one for the start, one for the finish); children make and use a right-angle tester (a 'Monster Right Angle Measurer') to find right angles in shapes and objects, and make right-angled turns between the four compass points.
learnerActions: Stand facing a chosen landmark (e.g. the window). Predict: how many quarter turns will bring you back to facing exactly the way you started? Say why before turning.
Make the turns one quarter at a time, always turning the same way (e.g. all clockwise), counting one right angle each time and noticing which way you face after each.
Pause after two quarter turns: notice you are facing backwards (a half turn / straight line), not home.
Link to the four compass points and a clock face: a quarter turn is one right angle, two a half turn, three a three-quarter turn, four a full turn (360°).
With a hinge or two geo-strips, open exactly to a right angle and connect: a quarter turn leaves a right angle between the start arm and the finish arm.
activities.intendedInsight: Turns are composed of right angles: two right angles make a half turn (facing back), three make a three-quarter turn, and four make a complete turn (360°) back to the start.

activities.title: Sort and classify mixed angles
feedback: You should select the tilted and long-armed right angles as well as the upright one — all three fit the checker exactly.
Leave out the just-less and just-more angles: the checker will not sit flush on them.
Justify by fit / quarter turn / square corner, not by which way the angle points or how long its arms are.
If you missed the tilted right angle, turn the checker to match its orientation and re-test.
activities.rationale: A mixed set including a tilted and a long-armed right angle lets the task discriminate a child who tests against the benchmark from one who recognises only an upright L or judges by arm length. Asking for the reason exposes whether 'right angle' means a quarter-turn / square-corner benchmark or merely a familiar picture.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should identify right angles, recognise that 2 right angles make a half-turn, 3 make three-quarters of a turn and 4 a complete turn, and identify whether angles are greater than or less than a right angle.

Children judge angle size by irrelevant properties including the length of the sides (a same-size angle drawn with longer sides is judged bigger), a misconception robust from preschool through elementary years; it stems from a whole-object assumption and is countered by framing angle as the measure of turn/opening.
learnerActions: Look at a set of about five angles laid out in mixed orientations: a true right angle tilted off-upright, a true right angle with very long arms, one angle just less open than a right angle, one just more open, and one obvious upright right angle.
Point to every right angle you can find, testing each with your checker rather than judging by appearance.
Sort the remaining angles into 'less open than a right angle' and 'more open than a right angle'.
Pick one angle you called a right angle and explain how you know — 'it fits my checker / it's a quarter turn / it makes a square corner'.
Order a few angles from least open to most open.
activities.intendedInsight: Classifying angles relative to the right-angle benchmark (less / equal / greater) establishes the less-than and greater-than idea informally, ahead of the words acute and obtuse, and relies on testing not appearance.

constraints: The right-angle concept is planar; turning in space or testing real 3D object corners can add interest but is not required to establish the benchmark idea.

Classification/counting questions (right / less / greater, order by openness, count right angles in a turn) can reliably assess understanding but do not by themselves elicit the hands-on testing of fitting a checker or the physical composing of turns — pair any such assessment with hands-on testing and turning.

A static picture that reveals 'right angle / not' when corners are tapped can support recognition and the small-square notation, but does not let a child test corners or compose turns; treat it as a partial scaffold for one facet only.
Deliberately include rotated/mirrored and long-armed right angles in any task so the benchmark is not tied to a standard upright L or to arm length.
When children predict turns, have them state the result relative to a stated starting direction (e.g. 'facing the window') so the count of right angles is unambiguous.
Keep child-facing language to 'less open' / 'more open' than a right angle at this stage; introduce acute/obtuse only as later vocabulary, not within these Year 3 prompts.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Removed the formal terms acute/obtuse from child-facing feedback to stay consistent with the stated goal of establishing less-open/more-open informally ahead of those words; retained them only as an adult note.

An optional on-screen version could use a draggable checker that glows green and stamps a small square on an exact fit (showing 'less open' / 'more open' otherwise) and a turn dial that adds quarter turns while a counter shows right angles (2 = facing back, 4 = home / 360°). These are illustrative interaction examples, not required mechanisms.

The source claimed 3D 'adds cost without deepening' and that an in-role dialogue 'cannot deliver' the felt fit of a checker; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited evidence and have been softened to scoped notes about affordances.

The source framed a quiz as assessing but 'not building checker intuition' — retained only as an objective limit that recognition/selection tasks do not themselves elicit hands-on testing; a selected-response format can still be used during teaching.
Efficacy phrasing in activity rationales was kept as 'intended/aims to' because these are unvalidated proposals; only the side-length-as-opening framing is directly supported by sources[2].claim.

assess.poeTask: Ask the child to PREDICT how many right-angle (quarter) turns it takes to end up facing exactly the way they started, and to say WHY, before doing it. Then have them make the turns one quarter at a time, counting a right angle each time and noticing where they face after two. A child who predicts two must confront landing facing backwards after two turns; the stated reason is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: This corner is tilted over on its side. Is it still a right angle? How could you check?
If you stand facing me and make two quarter turns, which way are you facing now, and how many right angles was that?
I drew this right angle with really long arms and this one with short arms. Is the long one a bigger angle? Why?
How is a right angle different from this one that's just a little bit more open than your checker?
assess.correctAnswer: Selects the true right angles regardless of orientation or arm length (including the tilted one and the long-armed one), leaves out the just-less and just-more ones, and justifies by 'it's a quarter turn / it fits my right-angle checker / it makes a square corner' rather than by how it looks or which way it points.

errorPatterns.pattern: A right angle must point up like an L; a tilted or mirrored one is not a right angle ('that one's on its side, so it's different')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rotate the checker itself onto the tilted corner so it still fits exactly — show the right angle is preserved under rotation; have the child re-test each corner with the checker turned to match.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Misses the tilted right angle and selects only upright ones

errorPatterns.pattern: The right angle with long arms is bigger / 'more than' a right angle ('its lines are longer so the corner is bigger')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Place the checker on the long-armed and the short-armed right angles in turn — both fit exactly; return to opening-not-length with the hinge.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rejects the long-armed right angle as too big, or ranks it as more open than the checker

errorPatterns.pattern: Any sharp-looking corner is a right angle ('that looks about square to me')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on the checker — place it and read 'more open' or 'less open'; build the habit of testing rather than eyeballing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Selects the just-less and just-more angles as right angles without testing them

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts right angles in a turn — two right angles make a full turn, or a half turn brings you back to the start
errorPatterns.nextMove: Physically make the turns, one right angle per quarter, marking each: two land you facing backwards (a half turn / straight line), four bring you home.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked to count right angles in a turn, says two make a full turn, or cannot say four make 360°

responseLevels.gap: Recognises only the upright L as a right angle, or labels corners as right angles by appearance without testing; miscounts right angles in a turn.
responseLevels.full: Uses the right angle as an orientation- and length-independent benchmark: tests any corner against it, classifies less/greater confidently, and explains a turn as built from right angles (two make a half turn, four a full turn / 360°), transferring to new corners and turns (relational).
responseLevels.partial: Identifies upright right angles, uses the checker on standard cases, and can recall that four right angles make a full turn, but treats these as separate skills — fails on the tilted or long-armed right angle, or cannot connect the quarter turn to the static square corner (multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Lay out about five angles in mixed orientations: a true right angle tilted off-upright, a true right angle drawn with very long arms, one angle just less open than a right angle, one just more open, and one obvious right angle. Ask: 'Point to every right angle you can find.' Then: 'Pick one you chose and tell me how you know it's a right angle.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Including a tilted right angle and a long-armed right angle separates a child who tests against the quarter-turn/checker benchmark from one who recognises only an upright L or judges by arm length. The tier-2 reason exposes whether 'right angle' means a quarter-turn / square-corner benchmark or merely a familiar picture.
